significance.justification: A verified-true result would establish that "linguistic form" and "functional-semantic reasoning" have causally dissociable circuitry, with form concentrated "early-to-mid," meaning later, and dissociation changing with scale; this is a form-(iii) layer-ordering/scaling claim combined with a nontrivial form-(ii) double causal decomposition. It would establish both a behavioral phenomenon—selective loss and sparing of grammaticality versus inference—and a mechanism fixing where and how the two computations diverge, directly bearing on the formal/functional distinction used by Mahowald et al. (2024), rather than merely showing that syntax is decodable as in syntax-localization work such as Lakretz et al. (2019). Verified false and verified true are distinguishable: failure of double dissociation would rule out this coarse independent-circuit explanation, although not every possible separation between language and thought; the qualifiers "partially" and broad "functional competence" modestly weaken determinacy. Topic substitution fails decisively: replacing these specific causal, layer-ordering, and scaling predictions with only "investigate language and AI intelligence" would not merit this score.

reach.justification: The named handles are the "double-dissociation index," "circuit overlap," and identifiable "form-circuit components" and "meaning-circuit" ablation targets. The ablation targets are ex ante interventions because they can be applied before model behavior to selectively alter one competence, although the proposed strengthening of functional competence is only suggested rather than itself specified as a demonstrated intervention. After per-model re-extraction, the conclusion still predicts a relation—form circuitry should be earlier, meaning circuitry later, and "scaling widens the functional gap"—so more than a search procedure transfers across sizes; likely downstream users include interpretability researchers and model builders, with no supported outside-AI uptake. The topic-substitution check again fails: the broad language–intelligence topic supplies none of these transferable metrics, intervention targets, or ordering predictions.
